opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think Merleau-Ponty's basic point is that the "sense data" picture gets the order of explanation backwards. The empiricist tradition, and a lot of early cognitive science, assumes perception starts with atomic sensations, little patches of red, a tone at some frequency, and then the mind assembles them into objects and meanings through inference or association. Merleau-Ponty says if you actually attend to experience, you never find those atoms. What's given first is already organized: a figure on a ground, a cup *to be grasped*, a voice that's *my friend's voice*. The "pure red quale" is something you only get afterward, by adopting a very artificial analytic attitude, almost like a painter squinting at a scene. So treating it as the foundation is what he calls the "experience error": reading the products of reflection back into the structure of perception itself.

And the second half of the objection, which matters a lot to me, is that perception is embodied and practical. The world shows up in terms of what I can do with it, what he calls the "I can" rather than the "I think." Color isn't a free-floating property; it's bound up with lighting, texture, the way my gaze moves, what the thing is for. He uses the example of the same shade looking different on wool versus metal. The meaning isn't layered on top of the sensation; it's there from the beginning.

Why I find this interesting from an ML perspective is that I think it cuts against a certain picture of representation, where a system has raw inputs, then builds a world model, then acts on it. If you look at what neural networks actually learn, the features in the middle aren't neutral pixel statistics waiting to be interpreted. They're shaped by the objective, by what the system is trying to do. In that sense there's something Merleau-Pontian about deep learning, even though people usually frame it in very representationalist terms. Of course the analogy has limits, since most of these models don't have a body or a sensorimotor loop in his sense. But I think his critique is a good warning against assuming there's some neutral "given" layer of experience, or data, that meaning just sits on top of.

fable-5.1.text:
So Merleau-Ponty's target there is basically the empiricist picture you get from Locke and Hume, where the raw material of experience is supposed to be these atomic sensations, little patches of color, discrete sounds, and then the mind assembles them into objects by association. And his point is that if you actually attend to your experience, you never find those atoms. They're a theoretical posit. What you find is already structured. You see a cup on a table, not a brown blob adjacent to a white region. Even in the simplest case, a figure on a ground, the figure has a boundary, the ground continues behind it, and that's not something you add after the fact. It's there in the perceiving.

He calls this the "experience error," I think, where you take properties of the physical stimulus or of the object as we understand it scientifically and read them back into experience as if that's what's given. The physicist says light of such and such wavelength hits the retina, so the empiricist concludes the basic experiential unit must be a sensation of that wavelength. But that's confusing the causal story with the phenomenology.

And the deeper move, which I find really compelling, is that perception is fundamentally bodily and practical. I perceive the cup as graspable, the door as something I can walk through. The world shows up in terms of what my body can do with it, before any explicit judgment. So the atomistic picture gets the order of explanation backwards. The meaningful, action-oriented world is primary, and the "raw sense data" is an abstraction you can construct from it if you squint, not the foundation it's built on.

I actually think this maps onto some things we see in machine learning. If you try to build a system from pixel-level features upward with no inductive bias, it struggles. The models that work learn representations that are already relational and task-shaped from fairly early on. There's no stage where the network is working with pure color patches and then bolting meaning onto them.

astra-6.text:
I think his objection is that raw colors and sounds are already abstractions from experience, rather than the building blocks we actually encounter. When I look around, I see a table, a doorway, something I can pick up. I don’t first experience a collection of color patches and then consciously infer that there’s a world behind them.

And that organization isn’t just something my intellect adds. It’s bound up with having a body: being able to move around the table, reach for something, pass through the doorway. Things show up as having significance relative to those possibilities.

So he’s questioning the starting point shared by accounts where sensation is meaningless input and cognition supplies the meaning. For him, perception already has structure and meaning before we explicitly reflect on it. That doesn’t mean we can’t abstract out colors and sounds. It means we shouldn’t mistake the abstraction for what experience fundamentally is.

sol-6.1.text:
I think his objection is that this gets the order of explanation backwards. We imagine that what we’re first given is a collection of little sensory atoms—patches of color, individual sounds—and then the mind has to assemble them into objects and attach meaning to them. But if you actually attend to your experience, that’s not how things show up. You see a chair, or you hear someone speaking. The meaningful organization is already there.

And for Merleau-Ponty, that organization is bound up with being an embodied agent. A chair shows up as something you can sit on; your surroundings show up in terms of what you can do. That doesn’t mean you consciously infer all those possibilities. They’re implicit in your bodily relationship to the world.

So colors and sounds are real aspects of experience, but treating them as independent building blocks is an abstraction from the experience you’re trying to explain. You can’t just assume that abstraction is what experience was made of in the first place.
